article_title: Replicating Experimental Impact Estimates with Nonexperimental Methods in the Context of Control Crossover (Working Paper)
citation: Brian Gill, Joshua Furgeson, Hanley S. Chiang, Bing-Ru Teh, Joshua Haimson, Natalya Verbitsky-Savitz. (2013). Replicating Experimental Impact Estimates with Nonexperimental Methods in the Context of Control Crossover. Working Paper 21. Cambridge, MA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Benchmark nonexperimental methods against experimental ITT estimates, accounting for control crossover
description: When judging whether nonexperimental methods can recover causal impacts, the article recommends using the experimental ITT estimate as the standard of comparison. It notes that "Ideally, nonexperimental methods that aim to replicate the results of rigorous randomized experiments focus on the intent to treat (ITT) experimental impact estimate," and that the comparison must handle "substantial control crossover" in the experiment.
requirements: Access to a rigorous randomized experiment providing an ITT impact estimate to serve as the replication benchmark
constraints: The principle is framed for experiments that include substantial control crossover, which complicates the comparison
target_learning_goals: selecting appropriate benchmarks when validating nonexperimental causal methods
examples: The working paper develops its replication approach specifically so that nonexperimental methods can be tested against experimental ITT impact estimates in crossover contexts

article_title: From High School to the Future
citation: Melissa Roderick, Jenny Nagaoka, Vanessa Coca, Eliza Moeller. (2009). From High School to the Future: Making Hard Work Pay Off — The Road to College for Students in CPS's Academically Advanced Programs. Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago, Urban Education Institute. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu
title: Benchmark advanced students' college outcomes by fully informed choice, not merely four-year attendance
description: The report recommends that for academically advanced students, schools and districts should measure success not by whether students attend any four-year college but by whether students and families make a fully informed choice among the wide range of accessible options. As it puts it, "our benchmark should be whether students and their families have made a fully informed college choice based on full knowledge of the wide range of college options available." This reframes college-going culture goals for high-achieving, largely first-generation populations.
requirements: High schools must fill gaps in student and parent understanding of college search, application, and selection, not only set college expectations
constraints: The report addresses a small group of programs and schools in CPS, though it argues lessons generalize as more schools build rigorous programs
target_learners: academically advanced high school students and their families
target_learning_goals: making informed college choices matched to qualifications
examples: The report urges practitioners building college-going cultures to meet the specific needs of academically advanced students rather than stopping at four-year enrollment

citation: Center on School Turnaround at WestEd. (2018). Thought Leadership Forum Brief: Turnaround Leadership and Leadership Competencies. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. http://centeronschoolturnaround.org
title: Behavioral Event Interview (BEI) as a competency assessment for selecting and developing turnaround leaders
description: The BEI is an in-depth interview method based on the assumption that past performance predicts future performance. A trained interviewer asks a candidate for detailed examples of past leadership successes and significant challenges, using probing questions; the interview may last up to two hours and concludes with a report including competency scores. Table 2 describes district uses in selection, onboarding/placement, and ongoing development and support.

constraints: The brief notes the BEI should be just one of a slate of indicators when used for selection
target_learners: Candidates for turnaround principal roles and the districts and states assessing them
target_learning_goals: Identifying leader competency strengths to inform selection, placement, and development
examples: New Mexico requires a BEI as an entrance requirement for all PPE participants and mentors; department staff conducted more than 100 BEIs over a six-week period for its most recent cohort

article_title: Bespoke: Generating MOOC-Quality Industry-Personalized Lecture Videos at Scale
citation: Romain Puech, Dewang Kumar Agarwal, Antonio Santamaría Escobar, Dimitris Bertsimas. (2026). Bespoke: Generating MOOC-Quality Industry-Personalized Lecture Videos at Scale. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26540
title: Bespoke: a five-stage pipeline that regenerates a complete industry-personalized lecture video from a seed transcript
description: Bespoke is a directed acyclic pipeline that takes a seed lecture transcript, a learner profile (healthcare, finance, energy, or generic), and a target duration, and compiles a new lecture video with slides, narration, and charts. Its five stages write audience-specific learning objectives, plan the lecture around a retrieved domain paper, write narration, build slides and charts in parallel, and reveal slide elements as they are spoken. Generation used Claude Sonnet 4.6 with GPT-5.2 validating in a bounded refine loop, following backward design and Mayer's multimedia principles. The article describes it as a pipeline that "regenerates a complete lecture video for a stated professional audience from a seed transcript".
requirements: A human instructor's seed transcript defining topic, scope, and the facts the new lecture may use
A stated learner profile and target duration
A bound of three refinement iterations to keep cost finite
constraints: All videos in the evaluation were generated without instructor intervention at generation time
The videos have no talking-head instructor
Mean API cost is about $0.22 per minute of video
target_learners: working professionals in healthcare, finance, and energy seeking upskilling
graduate analytics, machine learning, and optimization students
target_learning_goals: industry-appropriate understanding of technical topics such as decision trees, at audience-calibrated depth and with domain-relevant examples
examples: From 31 graduate seed lectures the pipeline generated over 200 videos across three industries plus a generic audience, at medium (5–15 minutes) and long (up to about 45 minutes) durations
In the running example, an iris-classification decision tree lecture was rewritten for clinical data scientists using a retrieved study on 30-day hospital readmission in heart-failure patients

article_title: Reducing Barriers to Academic Support: Evaluating a Course-Specific RAG System for Addressing Help-Seeking Disparities in Higher Education
citation: Andy Gray, Jake Hobbs. (2026). Reducing Barriers to Academic Support: Evaluating a Course-Specific RAG System for Addressing Help-Seeking Disparities in Higher Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21600
title: Beacon: a course-specific RAG academic support system grounding responses in approved teaching materials
description: Beacon is a web-based conversational support tool for computing students that combines a course-specific knowledge base with an open-source LLM. Rather than relying on the model's internal knowledge, "every response is generated using relevant teaching materials retrieved from the module knowledge base", so guidance stays aligned with module learning outcomes and assessment expectations. Its architecture comprises a curated knowledge base, a semantic retrieval component, an LLM, and a web-based user interface; retrieved passages carry source metadata so students can verify explanations against official module resources. It was built with open-source technologies (Flask, PostgreSQL with pgvector, Nomic Embed Text) allowing local or institutional deployment.
requirements: Only materials selected by the module teaching team are indexed, ensuring retrieved content remains course-specific and pedagogically appropriate; the knowledge base is updated when approved materials are added or revised.
constraints: The article states course-specific AI is not a substitute for effective teaching or student support services.
target_learners: undergraduate computing students in programming modules
target_learning_goals: programming concept understanding
assessment clarification
independent problem-solving and appropriate help-seeking
examples: The pilot used a minimalist Streamlit interface; Version 2 was reimplemented in Flask with a conventional chat interface displaying supporting source material alongside each response, and the model was upgraded from GPT-OSS-20B to GPT-OSS-120B.

article_title: Fear and Awe: Making Sense of Generative AI Through Metaphor
citation: Carmen Vallis, Stephanie Wilson, Alison Casey. (2025). Fear and Awe: Making Sense of Generative AI Through Metaphor. Journal of Interactive Media Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/jime.972
title: Move beyond binary permit/prohibit GenAI policies toward frameworks acknowledging both opportunities and ethical risks
description: The article argues institutional responses to GenAI should not reduce to permitting or prohibiting the technology. Instead, institutions could develop frameworks that acknowledge both opportunities, as the "augmenting device" metaphors suggest, and the ethical risks reflected in "black box" concerns. Metaphor workshops are proposed as a means of gathering diverse stakeholder perspectives, and programs should address the gap between anthropomorphic perceptions and GenAI's actual capabilities.
requirements: Institutional willingness to gather diverse stakeholder perspectives, e.g. through metaphor workshops, before policy formation
constraints: Grounded in findings from a single university business school context with a small student sample
target_learning_goals: ethical and equitable AI implementation in education
examples: The article suggests professional development could address specific fears surfaced through metaphors, such as anxiety about AI replacing teaching roles.

citation: Rose Niousha, Minwoo Kang, Narges Norouzi. (2026). INSIDE the Student's Mind: Jointly Modeling Latent Reasoning and Action in LLM Student Simulators. Published as a conference paper at COLM 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10492

citation: Naiming Liu, Brittany Bradford, Johaun Hatchett, Gabriel Diaz, Lorenzo Luzi, Zichao Wang, Debshila Basu Mallick, Richard Baraniuk. (2025). Learning Context: A Unified Framework and Roadmap for Context-Aware AI in Education. https://www.openstax.org

description: Belief-based models are a proposed LC component intended to capture learners' mental models, assumptions, preferences, and misconceptions—the beliefs that shape how they think, learn, and engage with content. The article positions them as under development: "we are working towards a BBM component that captures what learners actually believe." Their rationale is that beliefs shape learning trajectories in ways factual-knowledge modeling alone cannot capture, so beliefs must be represented as part of the broader Learning Context rather than only as mastered skills.

article_title: Behavioral clustering for adaptive learning object recommendation in higher education using learning analytics for personalized student success
citation: Najem, K., Zaoui Seghroucheni, Y., & Ziti, S. (2026). Behavioral clustering for adaptive learning object recommendation in higher education using learning analytics for personalized student success. Discover Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44217-026-02181-7
title: Behavioral clustering framework mapping learner profiles to adaptive learning object recommendations
description: A five-layer conceptual framework that translates data-derived learner profiles into learning object recommendations: data collection, processing with K-Means++ (k = 6), FSLSM-dimension mapping via affinity scoring, diversity regularization, and recommendation delivery with feedback capture. The article describes it as "a novel and interpretable mapping of behavioral profiles to personalized learning objects", connecting descriptive and predictive analytics to prescriptive, adaptive personalization. The affinity function uses a weighted Manhattan distance over five dimensions (engagement, performance, motivation, stress, resource access), with equal weights of 0.20, and the FSLSM mapping serves as a pedagogical interpretation layer rather than a psychometric classification.
requirements: Cluster centroids validated as pedagogically meaningful before mapping; a learning object catalog with attributes on the five affinity dimensions; a feedback loop for re-clustering in live deployment
constraints: The recommendation component is a proposed conceptual framework that "awaits empirical validation in live LMS environments"; clustering inputs are self-reported proxies rather than direct LMS interaction traces; FSLSM mapping values are heuristic scores not validated against a learning-style instrument
target_learners: higher education students in LMS-based and hybrid courses
target_learning_goals: personalized learning object recommendation matched to engagement, motivation, and performance profiles
examples: The worked example ranks LO_A (affinity 0.094) above LO_B (0.474) for cluster C0, confirming the formula behaves logically; Tables 9 and 10 assign each cluster a learning object type and engagement strategy

citation: Wang S and Zhao J (2026) Reflective AI use and student engagement in AI-supported programming: technology acceptance, programming self-efficacy, and behavioral trace evidence. Front. Psychol. 17:1929887. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1929887

description: This principle holds that mathematics and science instruction should start with concrete materials and then transition deliberately to abstract representations, rather than choosing one or the other. constraints: Recommended particularly for domains such as mathematics and science

citation: BERNEY, Sandra, BETRANCOURT, Mireille. (2016). Does animation enhance learning? A meta-analysis. Computers and education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2016.06.005

constraints: Limited to multimedia instructional material; findings characterize that body of studies rather than all animation use
target_learners: learners in experimental studies of multimedia instruction
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition from animated versus static graphic visualizations

article_title: When you know that you know and when you think that you know but you don’t
citation: Zechmeister, E. B., & Shaughnessy, J. J. (1980). When you know that you know and when you think that you know but you don't. Bulletin of the Psychonomic Society, 15(1), 41-44. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03334497
title: Do not rely on learners' sense of knowing for massed-repetition study: ease of re-encountering an item breeds unwarranted confidence
description: Because learners "think that they know" massed-presented items when they do not, self-assessments made immediately after massed repetition are unreliable guides for study decisions. The principle warns students and instructors that fluency at re-encountering material can produce undue confidence, so judgments of knowing should not be trusted for closely repeated material when deciding whether further study is needed.
requirements: A study situation in which learners monitor their own learning and allocate further effort accordingly
constraints: The article's evidence concerns within-list massed vs. distributed repetition of common nouns in free recall; the basis of the monitoring inaccuracy was not specified by the results
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment of learning
effective allocation of study time
examples: Students who claim after a poor exam, "I thought I really knew the material" may have equated time spent studying with amount learned while processing was inadequate for permanent memory registration

citation: Gasiewski, J. A., Eagan, M. K., Garcia, G. A., Hurtado, S., & Chang, M. J. (2012). title: Behavioral academic engagement in introductory STEM, measured as an eight-item student-behavior construct
description: The study operationalizes engagement as mainly behavioral, drawing on Fredricks et al.'s multifaceted construct that includes behavioral, emotional, and cognitive dimensions but focusing on observable academic task involvement. Eight items compose the factor: "frequency with which students asked questions in class, discussed course grades or assignments with the instructor, attended professor's office hours, participated in class discussions, tutored other students in their introductory STEM course, reviewed class material before it was covered, attended review or help sessions to enhance understanding of course content, and studied with students from their introductory STEM course." Principal axis factoring yielded a single factor (Cronbach's α = 0.75), with emotional-engagement items loading separately.

constraints: The construct intentionally excludes emotional and cognitive engagement, which the factor analysis showed load separately

target_learning_goals: Academic engagement behaviors supporting persistence in STEM majors

title: Judge course effectiveness relative to predicted DFW rates for the enrolled population rather than by raw DFW rankings alone
description: The article argues institutional attention should go to courses whose observed outcomes deviate from expectations. It predicts DFW probability per student using student type, life-cycle stage, prior GPA and prior DFW fraction, then computes the "difference (Gap) between them" to rank courses. This avoids misplaced or harmful fixes on courses simply serving a difficult population.
requirements: Predictive model of DFW probability per student using student type, academic-life-cycle stage, prior cumulative GPA, and fraction of previous courses with DFW grades
Institutional records linking end-of-term grades to courses over multiple years
constraints: Expected-rate approaches may need to differ across institutions based on local factors impacting student success
Very low observed DFW rates against substantial predicted rates may indicate grade inflation or concern rather than effectiveness
target_learning_goals: course completion
retention and degree completion
examples: Courses with alarmingly high raw DFW rates receded out of the alarm range when gaps were considered, and a mid-ranked course rose into the top 5 by gap
key_sources: Bloemer, W., Day, S., & Swan, K. (2017). Gap analysis: An innovative look at gateway courses and student retention. Online Learning, 21(3), 5-14. https://doi.org/10.24059/olj.v21i3.1233

article_title: Best Practice Framework for Online Safety Education: Results from a Rapid Review of the International Literature, Expert Review, and Stakeholder Consultation
citation: Walsh, K., Pink, E., Ayling, N., Sondergeld, A., Dallaston, E., Tournas, P., Serry, E., Trotter, S., Spanos, T., & Rogic, N. (2022). Best Practice Framework for Online Safety Education: Results from a rapid review of the international literature, expert review, and stakeholder consultation. International Journal of Child-Computer Interaction, 33, Article number: 100474. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijcci.2022.100474
title: Best Practice Framework for Online Safety Education: five elements with 22 effective practices
description: A multi-component national framework for online safety education in Australian schools (Foundation to Year 12), developed via rapid evidence review plus expert and stakeholder validation. The final Framework comprises 5 elements and 22 effective practices. Its elements are: students' rights and responsibilities; resilience and risk; effective whole school approaches; integrated and specific curriculum; and continuous improvement through review and evaluation. It is intended to support schools in teaching online safety, assessing program quality, and guiding best practice.
requirements: High-level framework intended to be universally applied to all school year levels, accompanied by implementation guides and support resources
constraints: Does not address what online safety might look like for children of different ages; developing a year-level curriculum was out of scope

digital citizenship
resilience and risk awareness
help-seeking and student agency

article_title: Behavioral economics of education
citation: Alexander Koch, Julia Nafziger, Helena Skyt Nielsen. (2015). Behavioral economics of education. Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization 115 (2015) 3–17. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jebo.2014.09.005
title: Behavioral economics framework for opening the soft-skills black box in education
description: The review proposes that concepts from behavioral and experimental economics—self-control (time-inconsistent preferences), willingness to compete, intrinsic motivation, and self-confidence—substantively describe what soft skills are and how they shape educational investments. It argues that economics of education often treats soft skills as a black box summarized by a parameter, and that 'applying models from behavioral economics and insights from laboratory and field experiments help us to better understand what is going on inside this black box'. The framework links these concepts to the education production function's family, school, and peer inputs.
requirements: Models must integrate behavioral concepts with standard economic theory and be validated empirically, as the article notes these assumptions 'also have to be validated empirically'
constraints: Experimental evidence mostly sheds light on short-run effects; lab and field experiments often use convenience samples, low stakes, and artificial tasks
target_learning_goals: understanding educational investment decisions and achievement through soft skills
key_sources: Alexander Koch, Julia Nafziger, Helena Skyt Nielsen. (2015). Behavioral economics of education. Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization 115 (2015) 3–17. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jebo.2014.09.005

article_title: Behavioral Economics of Education: Progress and Possibilities
citation: Adam M. Lavecchia, Heidi Liu, and Philip Oreopoulos. (2014). Behavioral Economics of Education: Progress and Possibilities. NBER Working Paper No. 20609. http://www.nber.org/papers/w20609
title: Design education policies around behavioral barriers: ease learning opportunities, remind students of long-term goals, build self-control, and encourage pride in skill development
description: The review argues that because behavioral barriers, not just returns and costs, shape education decisions, effective policy should reduce the effort of acting on learning opportunities and keep long-term goals salient. It states that "policies that make learning opportunities easier, continually remind students of long-term goals, teach strategies to develop self-control, and encourage youth to take pride in their own skill development are promising approaches for helping foster academic achievement". The principle treats small presentation changes as potentially powerful because they can produce large behavior changes at low cost.
requirements: Interventions must target the correct behavioral barrier; the review notes an ineffective nudge may simply have targeted the wrong barrier
constraints: A nudge that changes behavior does not necessarily prove the underlying intervention improves welfare, and researchers cannot at face value distinguish suboptimal choices from rational long-term weighing of costs and benefits
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
high school and postsecondary attainment
long-run education investment behavior
examples: The review cites automatic enrollment defaults in pension plans increasing savings significantly, and text-message homework alerts to parents, as behavioral policies with large effects from small changes
key_sources: Adam M. Lavecchia, Heidi Liu, and Philip Oreopoulos. (2014). Behavioral Economics of Education: Progress and Possibilities. NBER Working Paper No. 20609. http://www.nber.org/papers/w20609

article_title: Learning from others at work: communities of practice and informal learning
citation: David Boud and Heather Middleton. (2003). Learning from Others at Work: Communities of Practice and Informal Learning. Journal of Workplace Learning, 15, 5, 194-202.
title: Bernstein's construct of framing applied to communities of practice: strong framing means sharp boundaries on what is transmitted between members, weak framing blurred ones
description: The article imports Bernstein's (1990) construct of framing from studies of curriculum and schooling into the analysis of workplace learning networks. Framing of knowledge is strong "when there is a sharp boundary between what may be transmitted and what may not be transmitted in a learning relationship", and weak where the boundary is blurred. The authors identify strong framing with the tilers and weaker framing with the educational planners, and suggest loosely coupled communities of practice may be regarded as communities in which framing of knowledge is weak.
requirements: Applying framing requires identifying the boundary between what may and may not be transmitted within a learning relationship among network members.
constraints: The construct was developed from studies of curriculum and schooling; the article presents its application to workplace communities of practice as a proposal ('might also be applied').
target_learning_goals: Understanding the scope and consistency of knowledge transmission within workplace learning networks
examples: Strong framing was identified with the tiling teachers and weaker framing with the educational planners.
key_sources: David Boud and Heather Middleton. (2003). Learning from Others at Work: Communities of Practice and Informal Learning. Journal of Workplace Learning, 15, 5, 194-202. https://doi.org/10.1108/13665620310483895

article_title: How executive functions predict development in syntactic complexity of narrative writing in the upper elementary grades
citation: Drijbooms, E., Groen, M. A., & Verhoeven, L. (2017). How executive functions predict development in syntactic complexity of narrative writing in the upper elementary grades. Reading and Writing, 30, 209–231. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-016-9670-8
title: Developmental model of writing: transcription skills, oral language skills, and executive functions as interacting component skills within working memory
description: The article frames writing development with a developmental model (Berninger & Winn, 2006) in which "three interrelated component skills underlie written text production, as they interact functionally during the writing process in an environment of working memory (WM): transcription skills, oral language skills, and executive functions (EF)." The model specifies constraints influencing the writing process and postulates that the relative influence of each component changes over time: transcription is critical early, and its automatization frees WM resources for language skills and EF, which constrain later composition. The present study tests the model's longitudinal predictions in the upper elementary grades.
requirements: The model assumes a working-memory environment in which component skills interact functionally during text production
constraints: The relative influence of components is hypothesized to shift with development, so predictor importance is age-dependent
target_learners: elementary school children, particularly upper elementary grades (fourth to sixth grade)
target_learning_goals: written composition, especially narrative writing and syntactic complexity of sentences
examples: The study assessed all three components in fourth grade with a broad neuropsychological battery and tested their longitudinal prediction of sixth-grade narrative writing
key_sources: Drijbooms, E., Groen, M. A., & Verhoeven, L. (2017). How executive functions predict development in syntactic complexity of narrative writing in the upper elementary grades. Reading and Writing, 30, 209–231. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-016-9670-8

article_title: Children’s scientific curiosity: In search of an operational definition of an elusive concept
citation: Jirout, J. & Klahr, D. (2011). Children's scientific curiosity: In search of an operational definition of an elusive concept. Developmental Review (in press, draft). https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/developmental-review
title: Use behavioral rather than questionnaire measures to assess young children's curiosity
description: The review recommends assessing children's curiosity through observable exploration and information-seeking rather than self- or teacher-report questionnaires. Behavioral measures "do not require the same levels of comprehension skills and they measure actual exploration and information seeking, which is an essential manifestation of curiosity." The authors build their own preschool measure on this principle, grounding it in the information-gap framework.
requirements: Observable exploratory behavior must be measurable in controlled or naturalistic settings
constraints: Behavioral approaches trade off construct and ecological validity depending on how tightly controlled the situation is
target_learning_goals: measuring scientific curiosity and exploratory information-seeking
examples: The authors' new paradigm measures children's choices and exploration under varying levels of uncertainty
key_sources: Jirout, J. & Klahr, D. (2011). Children's scientific curiosity: In search of an operational definition of an elusive concept. Developmental Review (in press, draft). https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/developmental-review

article_title: The Psychology and Neuroscience of Curiosity
citation: Kidd, Celeste and Hayden, Benjamin Y. (2015). The psychology and neuroscience of curiosity. Neuron. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2015.09.010
title: Berlyne's two-dimensional taxonomy of curiosity: perceptual versus epistemic, specific versus diversive
description: The article describes Daniel Berlyne's classic taxonomy, in which he "distinguished between the types of curiosity most commonly exhibited by human and non-humans along two dimensions: perceptual versus epistemic, and specific versus diversive". Perceptual curiosity motivates seeking novel stimuli and diminishes with exposure, while epistemic curiosity aims at acquiring knowledge and applies predominantly to humans. Specific curiosity is desire for a particular piece of information; diversive curiosity is a general desire for stimulation, as in boredom. The authors note this categorization may be replaced by newer subtypes motivated by neural and developmental data.
requirements: Distinguishing curiosity types along the two dimensions as the article describes them
constraints: The authors anticipate Berlyne's categories will be replaced with differently-formulated subtypes motivated by new neural and developmental data
target_learning_goals: classifying forms of curiosity and information-seeking behavior
examples: Monkeys exhibit specific curiosity when solving mechanical puzzles without extrinsic incentive; rats exhibit diversive curiosity by preferring to explore unfamiliar maze sections
key_sources: Kidd, Celeste and Hayden, Benjamin Y. (2015). The psychology and neuroscience of curiosity. Neuron. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2015.09.010

article_title: Benefits of a bedtime routine in young children: Sleep, development, and beyond
citation: Mindell Jodi A., Williamson Ariel A. (2018). Benefits of a bedtime routine in young children: Sleep, development, and beyond. Sleep medicine reviews. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.smrv.2017.10.007
title: Conceptual model of bedtime routine benefits for broad child development (ages 0-5)
description: The article proposes a conceptual model (Fig. 1) in which "increased bedtime routine consistency and engagement in positive, healthy bedtime routine activities are critical in conferring improved developmental outcomes." Outcome domains are sleep, child mood/emotional-behavioral regulation, parent and family stress and functioning, and child language development/literacy/cognition, with child self-care/health and parent-child bonding/attachment hypothesized as additional outcomes. The model embeds the routine in a social-ecological framework with child, familial, and contextual factors, and excludes maladaptive activities such as television viewing. Mechanisms of action are deliberately not specified in the model.
requirements: Routine consistency (implementation on most nights) and engagement in positive, healthy bedtime routine activities
constraints: The model does not include specific mechanisms of action
Defined adaptive and maladaptive activities may not apply to all children; activities should be tailored to the individual child and family
The model is likely not exhaustive regarding outcomes
target_learners: caregivers and families of young children
target_learning_goals: healthy sleep
language development and literacy
emotional and behavioral regulation
parent-child attachment
family functioning
examples: The model's activity domains were selected based on cross-cultural commonalities in bedtime routine components shown in Figs. 2 and 3
key_sources: Mindell Jodi A., Williamson Ariel A. (2018). Benefits of a bedtime routine in young children: Sleep, development, and beyond. Sleep medicine reviews. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.smrv.2017.10.007

article_title: Benefits of a bedtime routine in young children: Sleep, development, and beyond
citation: Mindell Jodi A., Williamson Ariel A. (2018). Benefits of a bedtime routine in young children: Sleep, development, and beyond. Sleep medicine reviews. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.smrv.2017.10.007
title: Bedtime routine structured across four adaptive activity domains: nutrition, hygiene, communication, and physical contact
description: The article organizes common adaptive bedtime routine activities into "the broader domains of 1) nutrition, 2) hygiene, 3) communication, and 4) physical contact," each hypothesized to contribute to positive developmental outcomes. Examples include feeding or a healthy snack, bathing and oral care, reading and singing/lullabies, and massage, cuddling, or rocking. The domains were chosen based on cross-cultural commonalities in routine components and available early childhood research, and the authors note the list is not exhaustive and activities vary across cultures and contexts.
requirements: Activities occur in the hour or so before lights out, before the child falls asleep
Consistent nightly implementation of the routine
constraints: The list of activities is not exhaustive and activities may vary across cultures and contexts
Activities should be tailored to the individual child and family
target_learning_goals: sleep health
self-care and health habits
language and literacy
parent-child bonding
examples: Cross-cultural descriptive data showed feeding reported by 73% of families and bathing by 45% overall as routine components

article_title: Ethnic identity: Evidence of protective effects for young, Latino children
citation: Serrano-Villar, M., & Calzada, E. J. (2016). Ethnic identity: Evidence of protective effects for young, Latino children. Journal of Applied Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.appdev.2015.11.002
title: Bernal et al.'s developmental model of early ethnic identity: self-identification, constancy, knowledge, and preference
description: The study adopts a model of pre-adolescent ethnic identity, drawn from Bernal and colleagues and the social identity developmental literature, in which ethnic identity comprises self-identification, constancy, knowledge, and preferences. The article states the components "reflect a set of self-ideas about one's ethnic group membership" and that once ethnicity is integrated into the self, it guides information-processing toward ethnic-specific knowledge, behaviors, and feelings/preferences. The present study applies this model to MA and DA children aged 4–6 using a newly developed interview.
requirements: Requires children's emerging symbolic thought and social-category awareness, which the article locates in the early childhood years
constraints: The article notes the original model had not been subsequently tested before this study, leaving open replicability and generalizability to other Latino groups and contexts
target_learners: Young Latino children in pre-kindergarten and kindergarten (ages approximately 4–6)
target_learning_goals: Development of ethnic self-identification, constancy, knowledge, and preferences as components of social identity
examples: The study assessed each component with forced-choice and open-ended interview items, scoring self-identification and constancy dichotomously and coding knowledge and preference responses with trained bilingual coders (97% agreement)
key_sources: Serrano-Villar, M., & Calzada, E. J. (2016). Ethnic identity: Evidence of protective effects for young, Latino children. Journal of Applied Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.appdev.2015.11.002

article_title: The development of self-regulation across early childhood.
citation: Montroy Janelle J., Bowles Ryan P., Skibbe Lori E., McClelland Megan M., Morrison Frederick J. (2016). The Development of Self-Regulation across Early Childhood. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0000159
title: Behavioral self-regulation as coordinated integration of executive function skills into overt classroom behavior
description: The article frames behavioral self-regulation as a multi-component construct in which children coordinate executive function skills with motor and verbal functions to produce regulated overt behavior. It states that "Effective self-regulation in the classroom requires that the child seamlessly coordinate multiple aspects of top down control (i.e., executive function) such as attention, working memory, and inhibitory control along with motor or verbal functions". Development involves these initially separate skills becoming organized and integrated over time, with a qualitative shift between ages three and seven. The framework distinguishes cool executive functions, which the HTKS mostly draws on, from hot ones.
requirements: Assessment and support must address the integration of multiple executive function skills rather than single skills in isolation
constraints: The HTKS generally draws on cool aspects of executive function, though no task is entirely free of emotional context
target_learners: children ages three to seven in preschool through early elementary school
target_learning_goals: behavioral self-regulation for classroom functioning
examples: The study used the HTKS task, in which children must do the opposite of paired rules, to assess this integrated form of self-regulation longitudinally
key_sources: Montroy Janelle J., Bowles Ryan P., Skibbe Lori E., McClelland Megan M., Morrison Frederick J. (2016). The Development of Self-Regulation across Early Childhood. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0000159

article_title: Student Behavior and Epistemological Framing: Examples from Collaborative Active-Learning Activities in Physics
citation: Rachel E. Scherr and David Hammer. (2007). Student Behavior and Epistemological Framing: Examples from Collaborative Active-Learning Activities in Physics. Submitted to Cognition and Instruction. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Student+Behavior+and+Epistemological+Framing
title: Behavioral coding methodology for identifying epistemological framing in group video
description: A real-time observational coding protocol in which coders watch video of small groups without a transcript and note the exact time of changes in vocal register, affect, grammar, gesture production, and body language. Clusters are labeled with meaning-neutral labels (colors), at least two researchers code independently, and whole groups can be coded reliably because "peers typically share the same behavioral cluster." The method achieved 90% inter-rater reliability before discussion, to five seconds' accuracy.
requirements: At least two researchers code the changes independently; clusters are labeled with meaning-neutral labels before interpretation
constraints: The study's data set was a small, deliberately non-representative best-case sample of four hours from three groups in a well-functioning class with experienced TAs
target_learners: small groups of university students in collaborative active-learning activities
target_learning_goals: researchers' ability to observe students' epistemological framing during instruction
examples: Coding of group A's Newton's third law episodes, where the whole group shifted from blue to green behaviors at a transcript line

article_title: Productive dissent in learning communities
citation: Trninic, D., Swanson, H., & Kapur, M. (2018). Productive dissent in learning communities. Instructional Science, 46(4). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9466-0
title: Revisit the beyond-the-bounds principle: learners should seek ideas that challenge their beliefs
description: The article revisits Bielaczyc and Collins's beyond-the-bounds principle, which encourages individuals to question and actively challenge the results of communal negotiation. It emphasizes that learners "should seek ideas that challenge what they believe, by soliciting diverse opinions and views on a topic" and "should not just try to find support for their current beliefs." The principle frames dissent as a guard against jumping on the bandwagon of really bad ideas.
requirements: A community whose negotiation products can be questioned and challenged in search of something better
constraints: The article acknowledges no community stands entirely free of intolerance and authoritarianism; dogmatism may need continuous vigilance rather than elimination
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
a skeptical habit of mind
examples: The article points to the scientific community, which uses argumentation to reach consensus but also frequently challenges that consensus, as when one paradigm overturns another
key_sources: Trninic, D., Swanson, H., & Kapur, M. (2018). Productive dissent in learning communities. Instructional Science, 46(4). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9466-0

article_title: Effects of related decorative pictures on learning and metacognition
citation: Demian Scherer, Annika Verkühlen, Stephan Dutke. (2023). Effects of related decorative pictures on learning and metacognition. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09618-8
title: Behavioral measure of maintained situational interest based on choices of future seminar topics or take-home texts
description: The article operationalizes maintained situational interest not by verbal self-report but behaviorally: participants decided which of six described seminar topics (Experiment 1) or which of six take-home texts (Experiment 2) they wanted to engage with, and the count of yes-responses was the measure. The authors argue this is "not a merely verbal measure" but "a direct measure of whether participants want to engage further with this topic", providing a link to future interest-related behavior. The measure correlated significantly with topic interest and triggered situational interest in both experiments.
requirements: Participants must be able to choose among several genuinely related follow-up materials without inspecting them beforehand
constraints: In Experiment 2 the measure detected a reduction in maintained interest under pictures that the authors could not fully explain, calling it possibly "an incidental finding"
target_learners: university students in teacher education seminars
target_learning_goals: measuring maintained situational interest in learning research
examples: In Experiment 2, six take-home texts covered topics such as population policy in China, educational efforts in Tanzania, the carrying capacity of the earth, and world food; participants indicated yes or no for each text they wanted to take
key_sources: Demian Scherer, Annika Verkühlen, Stephan Dutke. (2023). Effects of related decorative pictures on learning and metacognition. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09618-8

article_title: Investigating students’ perceived authenticity of learning activities in an out-of-school lab for social sciences: a replication study
citation: Valentina Nachtigall, Nikol Rummel. (2021). Investigating students' perceived authenticity of learning activities in an out-of-school lab for social sciences: a replication study. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09556-3
title: Betz et al.'s three-part model of authenticity in teaching and learning contexts
description: The article uses the model by Betz et al. (2016) as its theoretical frame, "divided into three successive parts". Part 1 covers "the characteristics of learners and of learning settings that may have an impact on students' perceived authenticity"; Part 2 covers their interaction producing perceived authenticity; Part 3 summarizes outcomes affected by perceived authenticity. The study applies the model by varying only the method feature (PF vs. DI) while holding location, instructor, content, materials and innovation constant.
requirements: The model presumes perceived authenticity is produced by the interaction of learner characteristics and setting features, and mediates effects on motivational and cognitive outcomes
constraints: The article's test varied only the learning-activity (method) feature; other setting features were identical across conditions
target_learners: secondary school students (10th graders) in out-of-school labs
target_learning_goals: motivation (situational interest) and perceived authenticity of scientific inquiry practices
examples: The study operationalized the model's setting features in Table 4: method, location, instructor, content, materials, and innovation

article_title: Instruction, repetition, discovery: restoring the historical educational role of practice
citation: Trninic, D. (2018). Instruction, repetition, discovery: restoring the historical educational role of practice. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-017-9443-z
title: Bernstein's repetition-without-repetition explains how repetitive practice can be a fountainhead of discovery
description: The paper adopts Bernstein's notion of repetition-without-repetition as its explanatory framework: exercises repeat a form while varying the learner's engagement, so that repetitive practice can nonetheless generate discovery. The article states that “That repetitive practice can nonetheless be a fountainhead of discovery is explained using Bernstein's notion of repetition-without-repetition.” It uses this account to reconceptualize direct instruction, repetition, and discovery as complementary and synergistic.
requirements: Practice must be repetitive yet explorative, so that repeated exercises vary rather than merely duplicate performance.
constraints: The framework is elaborated through martial arts instruction and parallels in mathematics practice; the author notes that the trust dimension of practice while withholding information was not explored, calling it “a potentially significant limitation of present work.”
target_learning_goals: Developing proficiency through practice while making discoveries about the practiced activity
examples: The paper's empirical case is martial arts instruction in New York City and the San Francisco Bay Area, drawing on semi-structured interviews, video data, and training notes.
key_sources: Trninic, D. (2018). Instruction, repetition, discovery: restoring the historical educational role of practice. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-017-9443-z

article_title: Analyzing multimodal data to understand medical trainees' regulation strategies and physiological responses in high- fidelity medical simulation scenarios
citation: Moreno, M., Patino Melo, L., Grewal, K., Matin, N., Azher, S., & Harley, J.M. (2024). Analyzing Multimodal Data to Understand Medical Trainees' Regulation Strategies and Physiological Responses in High-Fidelity Medical Simulation Scenarios. Metacognition and Learning, 19, 1161–1213. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09403-z
title: Segmenting simulation scenarios into 'Beginning', 'Escalation' and 'Peak' for comparative multimodal analysis
description: A reusable analytic pattern in which a simulation scenario is divided into three scripted segments so behaviors, regulation strategies and physiological responses can be compared across critical points. The article explains: "We used the patient’s deterioration and scripted events to guide the segmentation of data, for example, we may use the “patient’s” sudden drop in pulse or the anaphylactic shock that tightens the airway to initiate the transition from the ‘‘Beginning’’ to the ‘‘Escalation’’ of a simulation." Segments were chosen for comparable length and to identify the stakes at each point, with the 'Peak' marking the convergence of medical decision-making and execution of patient care.
requirements: Scenario scripts or scripted patient-deterioration events to serve as event markers for segment boundaries
constraints: Many medical simulations lack a resolution segment, so the third segment ends at the 'Peak' rather than at a resolution
target_learners: Medical trainees working in teams in high-fidelity simulation scenarios
target_learning_goals: Understanding how team regulation strategies and physiological activation vary across phases of a simulated clinical task
examples: Raters negotiated segment boundaries jointly using each simulation's script, then compared code frequencies and APPS across the three segments

article_title: How Personality Matters for Education Research
citation: Hayley K. Jach, Lisa Bardach, Kou Murayama. (2023). How Personality Matters for Education Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09807-4
title: BESSI hierarchical framework organising socio-emotional skills into five domains aligned with Big Five traits
description: The review describes the BESSI framework (Soto et al., 2021, 2022), a hierarchical framework of socio-emotional skills built on a structure similar to the Big Five. It organises skills into five domains — "social engagement, cooperation, self-management, emotional resilience, and innovation skills" — each strongly positively correlated with a Big Five trait. The review proposes a conceptual distinction whereby traits describe average tendencies while skills describe the capacity to engage in certain emotions, behaviours, and cognitions.
requirements: Assessing both a BESSI skill domain and its correlated Big Five trait when researchers want to track whether developing capacity increases tendency
constraints: Positive correlation between a skill domain and a trait does not mean they describe the same thing, per the review
target_learners: school students in intervention and assessment studies
target_learning_goals: socio-emotional skill development including self-regulated learning, cooperation, and emotional resilience
examples: The review suggests assessing Big Five conscientiousness alongside BESSI self-management skills when studying whether capacity to work hard increases tendency to work hard

article_title: Fish swimming into the ocean: How tracking relates to students’ self-beliefs and school disengagement at the end of schooling.
citation: Dumont, Hanna; Protsch, Paula; Jansen, Malte; Becker, Michael. (2017). Fish swimming into the ocean. How tracking relates to students' self-beliefs and school disengagement at the end of schooling. The Journal of educational psychology 109 (2017) 6, S. 855-870. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000175
title: Berlin end-of-schooling tracking dataset (2,155 students, 87 schools)
description: The study's empirical basis combines "questionnaire, achievement, and administrative school data from 2,155 students from 29 low-track schools, 23 intermediate-track schools, and 35 comprehensive schools in Berlin, Germany." examples: The authors report the measure is largely robust to variations such as counting effort two days after the setback or defining setbacks as bottom-20% performances

description: A measurement protocol for stress in simulation-based training: STAI-Y administered before (T0) and after (T1) sessions, NASA-TLX at the end to assess mental workload, and five saliva samples collected "upon the arrival of the student, 10 min before starting the simulation, and then at 10, 20, and 30 min after the training". citation: Troost, A. A., van Ham, M., & Manley, D. J. (2023). Neighbourhood effects on educational attainment. What matters more: Exposure to poverty or exposure to affluence? PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0281928
title: Bespoke neighbourhoods of the 200 nearest households constructed with Equipop
description: A spatial operationalisation used to measure neighbourhood affluence and poverty for each individual and year. Equipop calculates the proportion of the k-nearest neighbours meeting user-set criteria — here, the ratio of poor or affluent households within the 200 nearest households for each year of an individual's life, based on geocoded 100x100m residential locations. Affluence is defined as household income above 150% of the year's median and poverty as below 60%, following the Eurostat at-risk-of-poverty definition. Constraining neighbourhoods to 200 households standardises measures across densely and sparsely populated areas and focuses on people rather than space.
requirements: Geocoded residential location data at 100x100m resolution and annual household income data adjusted to each year's median income
constraints: Neighbourhood income data were unavailable before 2003, so 2003 averages were used for 1995–2002, which the authors acknowledge as a limitation given neighbourhood change over time
target_learners: children and adolescents in the Netherlands whose neighbourhood exposure is being measured
target_learning_goals: measuring exposure to neighbourhood affluence and poverty across developmental periods to study educational attainment
examples: The study constructs annual affluence and poverty ratios for each of the 140,338 cohort members from birth to age 17, aggregated into early childhood (0–12), adolescence (13–17) and whole-childhood (0–17) exposure measures

description: Effective simulation debriefing feedback should focus on specific behaviours observed during the scenario, because "any comment will be specific and will refer to actions instead of talking about the person as a whole". constraints: The risk of being judgmental is high when providing feedback on colleagues' performances; dichotomous scales were perceived as too judgemental by respondents

target_learning_goals: metacognition and reflection on team dynamics and non-technical skills during debriefing
examples: In the MINTS-DR courses, peer observers filled in checklists after each scenario and provided feedback to colleagues during debriefing referring to their forms; the authors observed that prior to MINTS-DR the debriefing was often unbalanced and vague on non-technical aspects

title: Web-based computer-tailored nutrition education intervention 'Bewust eten, hoe doe je dat?' with basic and plus versions
description: The article describes a web-based computer-tailored nutrition education intervention called 'Bewust eten, hoe doe je dat?' ('Conscious eating, how do you do it?') consisting of four modules for fruit, vegetables, high-energy snacks and fat. requirements: A firm surface, a 46 × 46 × 13-cm medium-density foam block, a stopwatch for 20-second trials, and two independent investigators scoring errors.
